routes.description: Establish an objective standard under which unusual historical beliefs can be reasonable, show that the resurrection reports constitute admissible testimony, and argue that the relevant facts, expected evidence, and comparative explanations leave divine resurrection as a reasonable account.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if historical testimony can warrant an unusual event, the cited resurrection materials support sincere postmortem-experience claims, ordinary alternatives do not explain the relevant evidence equally well, and divine agency remains compatible with the applicable background knowledge and expected evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historical and explanatory case to the conclusion that believing Jesus rose can be reasonable without requiring personal conviction or certainty.

centralBridges.description: Supply a determinate standard for reasonable belief in an unusual historical event based on established facts, expected evidence, and comparative explanations.
Establish that the historical sources provide evidentially relevant testimony to sincere experiences and proclamations associated with Jesus after his death.
Show why legend, deception, error, hallucination, or transmission accounts do not explain the relevant testimonial and historical claims as adequately as resurrection.
Preserve divine resurrection as an available explanation by defending the possibility of divine agency and rejecting a presumption that natural regularity excludes exceptions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why testimony and historical inquiry can convey knowledge even when direct physical inspection or experimental replication is unavailable.
Clarify the evidential role of costly witness commitment and identify what kinds of contrary historical evidence could undermine the resurrection case.

routes.description: Distinguish the reasonableness of accepting resurrection from the event's truth, require evidence proportioned to background knowledge and the claim's unusual character, and argue that inaccessible testimony without adequate corroboration does not warrant accepting resurrection over ordinary human error.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available ancient reports cannot be sufficiently verified or corroborated, ordinary error or transmission remains more consistent with established experience, supernatural agency lacks independent warrant, and the evidence falls short of what accepting this unusual historical claim reasonably requires.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidential deficiencies to the conclusion that accepting the resurrection is unreasonable without undertaking to prove that it did not occur.

centralBridges.description: Ground reasonable acceptance in established knowledge about reality and require stronger support when testimony conflicts with well-supported background experience.
Show that ancient testimonial chains cannot be adequately identified, questioned, reconciled, or physically corroborated for the resurrection conclusion.
Maintain that mistake, deception, interpretive error, or distorted transmission remains a more warranted account of resurrection reports than a supernatural event.
Require independent demonstration of supernatural possibility before divine action can function as a warranted explanation of the historical reports.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Compare the surviving record with the stronger and more accessible evidence that a capable relational deity or a confirmed resurrection phenomenon could provide.
Separate evidence that witnesses sincerely held a belief from evidence that their interpretation of the reported experience was accurate.

sections.title: Reasonableness Standards and Debate Burdens
sections.rationale: The motion turns on the threshold for justified acceptance rather than solely on whether the event occurred, making the competing definitions of reasonableness, conviction, and burden foundational to every later issue.

sections.title: Historical Testimony and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: The resurrection case depends principally on ancient reports, so the evidential status of testimony, the accessibility and reliability of the sources, and the legitimacy of historical inference form a major shared issue.

sections.title: Resurrection and Ordinary Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing resurrection with error, deception, legend, hallucination, misidentification, and transmission accounts rather than assessing the reports without explanatory alternatives.

sections.title: Background Knowledge, Natural Regularity, and Divine Agency
sections.rationale: Whether resurrection is a live explanatory possibility depends on the role of established natural regularities, the warranted scope of scientific inquiry, and any independent basis for supernatural or divine agency.

sections.title: Expected Evidence, Corroboration, and Falsifiability
sections.rationale: The presence or absence of physical corroboration, accessible witnesses, modern confirmation, divine disclosure, and potential counterevidence bears directly on what evidence should be expected if the claim were true.

sections.title: Witness Sincerity and Evidential Sufficiency
sections.rationale: Costly commitment and multiple attestations may bear on sincerity, while the dispute over sufficient evidence determines whether sincerity and accumulated testimony can support the further resurrection inference.
